translations.text: In the very times of the kings who ruled the earth, in the reign of King Heraclius in Greece, King Arshak in Armenia and Varamshapuh in Persia, those holy bodies were offered as a sacrifice to the Lord.
It happened in the regions of the land of Armenia, in the times of the blessed and great Catholicos Nerses and of Adam Aregatsotel, in the valley of Basiani,
in a village called Onkom. There was a certain nobleman there, a duke (eristavi), whose name was Vardan, and his wife's name was Tagine.
Both of them came from royal families, and they held the true and right faith in the Holy Trinity.
They lived in the service of God, with all worthiness and fear of God.
And the Lord gave them two children, beautiful flowers, plants of the paradise of Eden.
And their parents rejoiced, because God had heard their prayers.
He gave them the two boys, and they named the firstborn David, after the great and radiant David
and the prophet David. And they named this second one too prophetically,
because he too was made worthy of the crown of martyrdom by the heavenly King. Although he lost this corruptible, passing world, he was made perfect in the one that does not pass away.
They named his younger brother Tirichan, in the Armenian language. The boys were brought up in the right faith.
Their mother's brother was Theodosius. He was a pagan and followed the lawless religion of the pagans.
While David and Tirichan were still small children, Vardan, the prince and duke, died,
and the godless Theodosius seized by force the domain of Vardan, his sister's son [sic], and took possession of their inheritance as well.
When that evil beast saw how beautiful those holy boys were, he thought:
"Perhaps later, when they reach full age, they will grow strong and rise up to do harm to me."
He could not restrain himself, but plotted a most wicked [?]. Taking their inheritance was not enough for him; he wanted to destroy them completely.
But blessed Tagine, worthy of God, heard of all the evil that was being stirred up against her.
And he said: "Abandon that religion of the Crucified One and hold to my religion, you and your children. Let those boys be my children, and I will raise them with delight and great joy."
But that blessed woman would not accept the utterly senseless [?] of that soul-destroying beast. Instead she said to him:
"Let this inheritance of my children and all their father's property be enough for you,
but the treasure that cannot be stolen and the inheritance that cannot be taken away, which come from God, the heavenly Father, you will not be able to take from me."
When he saw that this woman was firm in the faith of Christ, he spoke to her no more. Instead, without their mother, he summoned those blessed
boys, and with words that seemed sweet he wanted to turn them, so to speak, toward bitterness. And he thought in his senseless heart:
"I will test them in this friendly way, to see whether they will accept my religion and not hold resentment against me in their hearts."
He brought them, gathered them together and kissed them, as if out of love. But what he intended first was the death of their souls.
But when he could not achieve this, he plotted to kill them. He spoke to them like this: "You, children, are now my children, and from today I am like your father. Now what is mine is also yours.
Only do this for me: listen to what I tell you, as obedient and beloved children.
Abandon that faith which your father held, and I will give you a better faith."
After a silence, the holy children answered their mother's brother and said:
"The faith which our father held is enough for us, and we will remain in it as long as this soul is still in our bodies.
For the love of God and for endurance in him we are ready for anything except abandoning the faith, as our father was."

When the merciless Theodosius, whose bowels were of bronze, perceived this, he did not dare to kill them on this account, because of the Christian people. Instead he left them alone for a little while, though he still intended to destroy them.
Tagine, his mother, sensed this, and she considered where she might flee.
She took some of her possessions and her children and fled northward to the land of Tao. She came to a village called Vazhgani.
There was a prince there, a kinsman of the holy ones, whose name was Vazgen, and they put themselves under that prince's protection.
In the stronghold of that place they felt secure against the persecution of their mother's brother. They settled there and lived in the service of God.
She did not complain [?] about their dwelling or their life in a foreign land. Instead she rejoiced in that small and meager wealth, because the law of Christ was their delight and their riches.
Their mother also had a few sheep, and these blessed brothers would go out with them for recreation or to pasture them.

Those spotless lambs of God and true sacrifices would play with the lambs of the flock, and they exchanged their innocence with one another. Together they were being prepared as an offering to God Most High.
But Theodosius, their mother's brother, armed himself with wiles of many kinds, and he could not hide his anger, which raged like a wild beast's.
The children's escape from his hands grieved him, and their flight grieved his wicked heart.
He sent out his servants and spied on what the children did.
It was reported to that beast, who was watching for that innocent blood: "There is a high, gloomy mountain, and the children go up there with the sheep."
When they had learned this, he gathered many people and came cautiously and in secret, and they hid on that mountain, because it was waterless.
There was a tall forest there, waterless and impassable [?].
The mother called the children and sent them to the ravines of Vazhgani, as Jacob sent Joseph to the valleys of Hebron, and she said to them:
"Go, my children, and look after our few sheep."
They went joyfully and climbed the mountain. They raced one another for fun, and in this way they went up [?] to the summit of that mountain.
But the tyrants were lying in ambush like lions. When the children had come only halfway, the men in ambush shouted and surrounded them.
And Theodosius, their maternal uncle, rushed out and ran at them to destroy them.
Now the innocent boys were eating bread with milk, for they had let their sheep lie down to rest. And the boys trembled and were startled, and they began to look around, and did not know the reason.
But blessed David recognized his maternal uncle and was comforted, and with a cheerful face and a sincere heart he ran and threw himself into his uncle's arms.
And he stretched out his hands and lifted him up in his arms, and instead of a kiss he gave him the sword: he struck him and killed him.
And the martyrdom was completed, and he quickly found the way to heaven and won the crown of martyrdom.
Now the staff that slipped from his hands was of walnut wood; it fell to the ground and became a great tree on that mountain.
And that tree stood for about two hundred years, and pilgrims carried it away as a blessing (eulogia).
But when Tirichan saw the merciless death of his brother, he was afraid and hurried to flee.
He headed toward the ravine, westward to the village called Divri, which people call by the name of the devs [?].
And when the ruler perceived this commotion and saw men like enemies coming up with weapons and swords,
he began to cry out and quickly gather the people, for he thought that they were coming to kill him. He quickly made ready to fight them.
But the pursuers overtook holy Tirichan and killed him, and they left him and turned back themselves. And the ruler was amazed at their sudden return.
And the men of that place came and saw the boy lying on the ground, wounded with cruel wounds, and his soul stirring to depart to its Creator.
They pitied his youth, and they did not know the cause of his death.
Then the ruler of Divri also arrived and saw the innocent blood that had been shed; he was amazed, and great astonishment seized him.
And at once the women of that place also arrived, and there was great weeping over the boy.
But when Tirichan's killers arrived and climbed the mountain, they found their chief Theodosius, for he was in distress and could not see at all.
And astonishment seized these men too; they stood dumbfounded.
And the crowd of people was also troubled, and they began to grieve and to grow faint at the wonder they had seen.
They trembled and could neither speak nor flee, for their leader had been taken from them [?], and he was struck with blindness, like the blessed Paul,
when he had rushed against the divine teaching, and at once [God?] put the bridle of His mercy on his mouth,
so that his wild, deranged mind might turn back and he might be able to come to his senses
about what he had done; for he thought: "We have done nothing improper, for I have killed my sister's sons."
For in this way too he resembled Paul, since Paul also killed his sister's son, Stephen the Protomartyr.
And straight away the ruler of Divri mounted his horse and went up with his people onto that very high mountain, in order to see those people and learn the cause of that disturbance.
And when she saw that the people had gone up and that their chief was sorrowful, and behold, the [?] of that uproar reached her,
the uproar that had arisen over the sons of the blessed Tagine, the woman Tagine rose up and hurried up the mountain.
And she came and arrived, beating her face. On that very steep slope she did not tire, because of the pain she felt for her sons.
She cried out with weeping and with an embittered soul. She tore her garment and said to her brother Theodosius: "Why have you taken from me the lights of my eyes?
Was this widowhood of mine not enough for me to mourn? Was the inheritance of my children not enough for you, and my living in this dark land?

Could you not be satisfied with my husband's inheritance? Instead you came into the wilderness and slaughtered these lambs that followed the sheep, and struck down both of these innocent shepherds, and their flocks are left in the wilderness without a shepherd.
"Theodosius, you merciless beast, what evil did these sons of mine ever do to you?
Why have you darkened my sun at the very first hour of the day, and still you have not ceased persecuting me?
Was this one not enough prey for you, you evil beast? You should have left me one and taken pity on this widowhood of mine!
Now who will be my hope or my trust? Kill me too, you godless one, and glut yourself with blood, you tiger, lover of blood!
I will no longer go away from this mountain. Just as during my sons' lives I rejoiced to see them, so now let my death be together with their death.
Let my soul die with the soul of the righteous, and let our bodies lie in one grave, just as during the life of my widowhood we had one bed.
"Theodosius, do you no longer remember the womb of the mother who bore you and me, and the breasts that nursed you and me?
Utterly hard-hearted one, why have you come out with so many people to make war on a weak woman and her [?] children?
Why have you put out these lamps of mine, O lawless one?" The blessed Tagine spoke these words and others like them.
And the whole multitude of people were silent and lamented, and shed tears like streams. And Theodosius too wept with them.
When the blessed Tagine saw her beloved son David lying slain, her eyes darted about and she searched for her son Tirichan,
so that she might see him too lying slain, but he was not there. And her heart was stunned by that distress and anguish.
And Theodosius could not understand that blindness. At that moment Theodosius began to speak and said to his sister Tagine:
"O my sister Tagine, turn to me and see: here on the summit of the mountain darkness has covered me, as if I were in deep ravines, or in a pit, in the abyss.
Thick darkness turns upon me, but for you a light has shone forth from the unapproachable light, from the unfading and true, the endless light.
But now have mercy on me, this merciless and unworthy one! Do not repay me according to my deeds. Instead, entreat the holy martyrs to show mercy to me,
so that I, who am unworthy, may be made worthy of the seal of Christ, the merciful God, who came for the sake of sinners. I believe in the true God."
And when she came to her senses and saw that her beautiful lambs, her children, had been offered as a sacrifice to God, she was at once filled with joy and quickly cast off
the grief of her pain for her children. And in that same hour joy overtook her mourning, and she kissed her brother and said to her brother:
"May God forgive you, and may the merciful Lord not count against you the death of my children, your sister's sons,
just as once [it was not counted against] Paul [?], [in the case of] his sister's son Stephen, the first deacon and first martyr."
She prayed to God, lifted her eyes to heaven, blessed the Lord, and held back her tears,
so that He would not count the ember of her mind as nothing, and so that her incense would not fail to spread its fragrance. And that woman Tagine said:
"You, Lord, merciful in every way and compassionate to all, Father of orphans and Judge of widows,
who did not disregard these little and humble boys, and made them sharers in the portion of the holy martyrs —
these my children, who endured many torments for your sake and received the unfading crown of heaven and the life that does not pass away —
the martyrdom of these in their childhood: make them worthy to be with them in delight and joy, and with them in rest, and with them in the crown,
and with them in the healing of the suffering — as those, so also these. And so that I may know that they have been pleasing to you, grant healing also to this my brother, so that he may see."
And she took the earth that had been soaked with David's blood and anointed his eyes, and at once his eyes regained their sight.
These two miracles took place over Saint David.
And again God, the lover of mankind, saw fit that, in order to all
people reveal their courage and make known that God had been pleased with the sacrifice of their martyrdom, on that night lights shone forth
like stars, in the form of a pillar of light, whose top reached up to heaven, which all the peoples of the land saw;
and those who knew glorified God, and those far away who saw that light marveled and questioned one another.
Then, when this matter became known to our holy father Nerses, Catholicos of Armenia —
for he himself saw from Ishkhan the marvel and the incomprehensible brilliance of the light by which the Lord glorified His worthy ones —
he understood this matter through the Holy Spirit and hastened to Divri, and brought with him the priests John, Sahak and Gregory.
And Theodosius fell at the feet of Catholicos Nerses and confessed all the sins he had committed, and received the seal of Christ,
and believed with all his heart in our Lord Jesus Christ and in all His martyrs and saints.
And the holy Nerses with his own hand wrapped the bodies of the saints, with Tagine their mother and Theodosius standing by,
and he laid one of them on the mountain and the other below Divri, to the west, in the ravine of the stream-bed.
And Theodosius spent money and built a church over David, and he kept and established their commemoration.
And the prince of Divri took away portions of the holy bones of Tirichan, and he too built a church as a martyr's shrine for him. It was built within his territory, among the vineyards.
And the blessed Tagine went to the valleys of Mamorvani, to a village called Tadzarani, and there he died.

And his tomb also brings forth healing. And the prince of Divri built a church among the vineyards to the glory of the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit, now and always and to the ages of ages. Amen.
